job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Diego Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Fermoy and take the 7:40 train to Cork most mornings. I'm doing a master's in electrical power systems, so I'm in lectures on grid stability or in the lab running simulations until about four. I'm home for dinner, and then I either study at the kitchen table or help my little sister Aoife with her nursing coursework. I did three months at a regional grid operator last summer, drawing substation layouts, and I keep half hoping they'll call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about right, because the grid still needs engineers who can stand in a substation and understand it. To friends I'd say the hype was always louder than the product. Online I'd probably say nothing, because I don't want to sound like I'm gloating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd say it's the best case for me. Power systems is one of the few areas where graduates are still wanted, because of wind and solar connections. My worry is not AI, it's whether the operator I interned with has a graduate place, and I don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's in June and apply to the grid operator and to two wind developers near Cork. In the meantime I'd keep my part-time lab assistant job, which pays a few hundred a month. I'd also use the AI tool I already use now and then for debugging my MATLAB scripts, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. My dad, Tommy, drives a bus and he's a union rep, so I grew up with the idea that a steady job is something you keep an eye on. But I'm living at home with low costs, so I'm not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hope the grid operator calls. What's the uncertain part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the one at the grid operator. My manager there, Siobhan, said they only decide on graduates once the budget is signed, usually in spring. If they say no I've still got the wind developers, but I'd prefer the grid because it's public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money tightens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The train pass, about a hundred and twenty a month. Then I'd stop going out on Saturdays. I owe around fourteen thousand in loans, which isn't nothing, but my parents have said they'd help for a few months if I needed it.

say: I'd say that's about right, because the grid still needs **engineers** in the field.
I'd tell friends the hype was always **louder** than the product.
think: I think this is the **best case** for me, since power systems still wants graduates.
My worry is the **graduate place** at the grid operator, not AI.
do: Finish the master's in June and apply to the **grid operator** and two wind developers.
Use the AI tool only to **debug** MATLAB scripts.
feel: I feel **calm**, because living at home keeps my costs low.

fieldNote: Diego is **calm** because his field is in demand and his costs are low.

He is wary of looking like he's **gloating** about a quiet outcome.

steps.text: Finish the power systems master's in June
Apply to the grid operator and two wind developers near Cork

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's going to be uneven, and the people who write the rules matter more than the machines. Software doing the drawing checks is fine, if the savings don't all go to the shareholders. I'd say we need agreements with unions about how it's introduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the substation drawings I did over the summer are exactly what a tool will do. A senior engineer, Fergal, already told me the juniors used to spend a year on drafting and now it's a month. So fewer junior hires, I think, and I'd be one of the juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the planning and simulation software the operator uses, and take the course their engineers took. I'd ask Siobhan to let me shadow a site commissioning, because that's work software can't do for another few years. And I'd start putting two hundred a month away, because loans don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. There's no panic, because I don't think the industry will stop building wind farms. But it's strange to learn you were trained for the job that's shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your senior engineers about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the AI company or the engineer takes the blame when a drawing is wrong. Years ago a bad drawing meant a person could be named. I'd want the union to insist a named engineer signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you feels it most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my friend Ciaran who did computer science. He had no job offers by Christmas. He says employers asked if he could do prompt writing instead of coding, and that was it.

say: I'd say the **rules** matter more than the machines, and unions should agree how it's introduced.
I'd say savings must not all go to **shareholders**.
think: The **substation drawings** I did last summer are exactly what a tool will do.
I'd be one of the **juniors** who are hired less.
do: Ask Siobhan to let me shadow a **commissioning** on site.
Put **two hundred** a month into savings.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, because I was trained for a job that's shrinking.

steps.text: Take the operator's course on power system simulation software
Shadow a substation commissioning with Siobhan at the grid operator
Save two hundred a month from lab assistant pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough for anyone to be fair about it. We'd need a public plan and some income guarantee, because families can't plan their rent around a prediction. I'd get my dad's union involved if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a degree that arrives just as the work leaves. Even the field bit, like standing in a substation, is only three years behind. I might get a few years of work, but not a career, and the loans still run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to everything, both the grid and the contractors, and take any work on site. I'd save every euro and cut out the train pass by cycling the first leg. I'd also join a union and the energy graduates' group on day one, and call my local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly frightened, if I'm honest. I'd keep a calm face for my mum, who worries enough about Aoife's course. At night I'd be doing sums on how long fourteen thousand lasts without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Aoife?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Aoife, my sister. Nursing is hands-on, so it's safer for longer, and I'd tell her to stay in it and not worry about me. I'd tell my parents we'll pool money and that I'm not too proud to ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap for robots change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practical part, like site work, three years later. That gives me a thin window. I'd rather be a graduate who got a site job in year one than one who held out for a design office.

I'd ask my dad's **union** to take it up.
think: I'd have a degree that arrives just as the **work leaves**.

feel: I feel **properly frightened** and keep a calm face for my mum.

fieldNote: Diego's **steadiness** shows in practical choices, not denial.

steps.text: Apply to site contractors as well as the grid operator
Cycle the first leg of the commute to cut the train pass

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it to pass proper laws about who owns the gains. At work I'd push the union to bargain about it now. To friends I'd say start learning the tools, and don't sneer at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly I think I'd have a decent run first. I'd be twenty-nine by 2031, with about four years of experience under me and probably a job in the field. After that it's less clear, but I'd have savings and some choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take the first power job, probably the grid or a wind developer. I'd put away about a third of my pay for four years and learn the AI tools properly at work, once the firm's own people have used them. Maybe study for a chartered engineer title in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not scared. The time lets me plan, and I like plans that I can write on paper. But I'd still keep checking whether my firm is hiring or firing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first, and what would you wait on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My dad's depot is already testing a route-planning program, and a union rep like him wants a say in it. If I'm paid and he's got a pension, I can help Aoife through nursing school and maybe a deposit for something small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family fit into the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the hands-on side, then add the planning side as the tools get reliable. Steady is how I do things: I don't jump first, but I don't dig in either.

I'd tell friends to **learn the tools** and not sneer at them.

steps.text: Take the first power engineering job at the grid or a wind developer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough that nobody has an excuse. We should be building retraining and a shorter working week now. I'd also say energy and the grid should stay publicly owned, so the gains aren't taken privately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think that's the most manageable one. I'd be thirty-four and well into a career, maybe leading a team of field engineers. The thinking part of my job will change, but I'd have a decade to turn into somebody who checks and directs the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, work for the grid, get chartered and learn the AI side as it matures. I'd save for a house deposit near Fermoy. I'd also stay in the union and go to the branch meetings, because a decade is when rules get written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. A little nervous about what happens to people who don't see it coming, like some of my dad's friends at the depot. But for me, it feels like it's survivable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Aoife about her nursing course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Aoife to take up nursing and maybe specialise in something with technology, like monitoring. And I'd tell her that any job that's about people is safer. She doesn't need persuading, she's much more stubborn than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about in that long window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My dad's depot friends, who are all in their fifties and don't use computers much. Ten years should be enough for them to retire, but not for everyone. I'd want some training scheme for them through the union.

I'd say the grid should stay **publicly owned**.

steps.text: Work towards chartered engineer status while employed at the grid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. There's no time to build a plan and no way to ask my parents for much. What would help is an income guarantee, public training places and a firm that tells people early. I'd also want my union at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that my generation gets told it's lazy or fragile when really we're doing what we were told: study, borrow, hope. Where I live, the sums are real. I'm not against the tools, I'm against being left to carry the bill on my own.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the tools, I'm against being left to carry the bill on my own.
portrait: Diego is a **24-year-old** electrical power systems master's student in Cork, living with his parents in Fermoy.
He owes about **fourteen thousand** and has one internship at a grid operator, plus a lab assistant job.
His family's **union** roots shape his views: rules, public ownership and shared gains.
He is steady, trying AI tools once they're proven, and his mood moves from **calm** to anxious only with two years.
He thinks of the whole household, especially his sister **Aoife**, when he plans.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because there'd be no time and his family couldn't carry him for long.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee**, public training places, early honest warning and a union at the table.
